title: Secrets, hashing and encryption basics
description: The difference between encoding, hashing and encryption, how passwords should be stored, and how to keep keys and secrets out of the wrong places.

questions.text: Which statements about encoding, hashing and encryption are correct?

options.text: Base64 is an encoding, so anyone can turn it back into the original data without a key
A hash is one-way: you can compute it from the data, but you cannot recover the data from it
Encryption is one-way, so encrypted data can never be read again
Hashing and encryption are the same thing, because both scramble data

questions.explanation: Encoding such as Base64 only changes the format, so it hides nothing, and a hash is a one-way fingerprint that has no key. Encryption is the reversible one: with the right key you get the original back. Mixing them up leads to mistakes like 'protecting' a secret with Base64 or hoping to decrypt a hash.

questions.text: Why should a login system store a hash of each password rather than an encrypted copy of it?

options.text: Hashes are smaller, so they take up much less room in the users table of the database
Encrypted passwords cannot be compared with whatever the user types in at login time
Encryption is far slower than hashing, so each login would take much too long to finish
A hash is one-way, so a stolen database cannot simply be decrypted back into passwords

questions.explanation: To log someone in you only need to check a guess, which you can do by hashing the guess and comparing hashes. With encryption, anyone who steals the database together with the key, which the server must keep somewhere, gets every password back. Size and speed are not the reason.

questions.text: What does adding a unique random salt to each password before hashing achieve?

options.text: It makes each hash faster to compute, which cuts the login time on the server
Equal passwords end up with different hashes, and precomputed tables become useless
It acts as a secret key kept outside the database, so a stolen database cannot be cracked
It encrypts the hash so that only the application server is able to read it

questions.explanation: A salt is a random value stored next to the hash; it is not secret. It makes every hash unique, so an attacker cannot reuse one table of precomputed hashes against all users or spot who shares a password. A secret kept outside the database is called a pepper, which is a different tool.

questions.text: Why is a single round of SHA-256 a poor way to store passwords, when bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 are recommended?

options.text: SHA-256 has been broken, so attackers can simply reverse every hash back into a password
SHA-256 cannot be used with a salt, so equal passwords always give the same hash
SHA-256 is designed to be fast, so attackers can test billions of guesses per second
SHA-256 output is too short to tell different passwords apart with any real reliability

questions.explanation: Password hashes are deliberately slow (and, for scrypt and Argon2, memory-hungry), with a cost setting you can raise as hardware improves, so a thief with a leaked database must pay heavily for every guess. SHA-256 is not broken and can be salted; it is just far too cheap to compute for this job.

questions.text: How does a TLS (HTTPS) connection use asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?

options.text: Public-key methods verify the server and agree a key; symmetric encryption protects the data
Symmetric keys prove the server's identity, and asymmetric keys then encrypt all of the traffic
Asymmetric encryption protects every byte of the traffic, because it is the stronger kind
Only symmetric keys are used, and the certificate is a password that the user types in

questions.explanation: Asymmetric (public and private key) operations are comparatively slow, but they let two strangers prove identity through the certificate and agree on a secret over an open network. Symmetric encryption with that shared key, such as AES, is fast, so it carries the bulk of the traffic. Nobody types a password for this.

questions.text: A service sends webhooks with a plain SHA-256 hash of the body in a header, so receivers can detect tampering. Why is that not enough?

options.text: SHA-256 is too weak for tamper detection, so a longer hash such as SHA-512 is needed
Whoever changes the body can compute a new hash; an HMAC needs a shared secret key
HTTP headers are not allowed to carry hash values, so the hash must go in the body
It is enough, because a one-way hash cannot be forged by someone who changes the body

questions.explanation: A plain hash has no key, so an attacker who edits the body simply recomputes the hash and swaps it in; being one-way does not make it unforgeable. An HMAC mixes in a secret shared by sender and receiver, so only a key holder can produce a valid tag. A longer hash without a key has the same flaw.

questions.text: A team can safely design its own encryption scheme, as long as it keeps the algorithm secret.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Security should rest on the secrecy of the key, never on hiding how the scheme works, and home-made schemes almost always hide subtle flaws that only experts find. Use well-reviewed algorithms such as AES-GCM through a trusted library, and let the library handle details like nonces.

questions.text: Which of these are sensible ways to give a deployed service its database password?

options.text: Store it in a secret manager and let the service fetch it when it starts
Put it in a config file in the repository, because the repository is private
Set it as an environment variable in the deployment, outside the code and the image
Copy a .env file that contains it into the container image

questions.explanation: Both good options keep the value out of the code and out of the image: a secret manager adds access control, audit logs and easy rotation, and an environment variable set at deploy time is a simpler step up, though it can show up in process listings and crash reports. Anything copied into an image or committed to a repository lives on in image layers and git history, available to anyone who can pull them.

questions.text: A developer commits an API key to a repository and deletes it in the next commit. What should the team do?

options.text: Nothing is needed, because the latest version of the file no longer contains the key
Make the repository private, because the key then stays safe from now on
Treat the key as leaked: revoke it, issue a new one and store that one safely
Rewrite the git history with a force-push, then carry on using the same old key

questions.explanation: Git keeps every earlier commit, and clones, forks, caches and bots that scan public repositories may already hold the key, so deleting it from the latest commit protects nothing. The safe response is to revoke and replace (rotate) it, then clean the history and check the logs for misuse. Planned rotation works the same way, with the old and new key valid side by side for a while so nothing breaks.

questions.text: A password-reset token generated with Math.random() or a timestamp is safe as long as the token is long enough.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Ordinary random functions and timestamps are predictable: an attacker who sees some outputs can often work out the next ones, so extra length does not help. Use a cryptographically secure generator, such as crypto.randomBytes in Node, secrets.token_urlsafe in Python or the operating system's random source.
